This process can take a few minutes the first time.
Once Kubernetes is up and running, you can verify the installation with the following command:

This indicates that your local cluster is healthy and ready to accept workloads. From now on, any kubectl
command you run will target this local cluster unless you explicitly change the context.
Running i d x _ 6 6 b d 6 6 5 f Kubernetes through Docker Desktop has several i d x _ 3 d 5 a 0 2 e 2 advantages. It is tightly integrated with your existing
Docker installation, supports both Linux and Windows containers, and requires no additional setup. You can build,
test, and deploy directly from the same environment without switching tools.
483 Introducing Kubernetes
Running Kubernetes with minikube
minikube is i d x _ 9 8 6 3 b 3 a 7 another excellent option for running Kubernetes locally. Unlike Docker Desktop, which hides much of
the setup, minikube gives you full control over how your cluster is created. It can use different virtualization
backends (such as Docker, HyperKit, VirtualBox, or KVM) and allows you to configure multiple profiles, resource
limits, and add-ons.
To install i d x _ d c 8 6 6 1 d 7 minikube, follow the instructions for your operating i d x _ f b 2 4 2 f 4 1 system at https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/
start/.
Once installed, start a new cluster by running the following:
$ minikube start
This command downloads a small VM image, boots it, and sets up a single-node Kubernetes cluster inside it. In
your terminal, you should see something like this:
Figure 15.5 – Starting minikube
You can verify that everything is working by running the following:
$ kubectl get nodes
You should i d x _ 1 5 b b 6 2 e d see a node named minikube in the Ready state. To i d x _ 7 1 5 2 1 2 c e stop the cluster, run the following:
$ minikube stop
Run the following to delete it completely:
$ minikube delete

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 484
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 484
minikube also includes a rich set of add-ons for common use cases. For example, you can enable an ingress
controller or a local metrics server with simple commands:
$ minikube addons enable ingress
$ minikube addons enable metrics-server
To access a web dashboard for your cluster, use the following:
$ minikube dashboard
This opens i d x _ 8 3 3 9 0 6 b 9 a browser window showing the Kubernetes i d x _ 8 d 0 5 a e c 3 Dashboard UI, which provides a graphical overview of your
cluster's workloads and resources.
minikube is ideal if you want to understand how Kubernetes is set up and gain hands-on control over cluster
configuration.
Running Kubernetes with kind
kind, short for Kubernetes in Docker, is a lightweight tool that runs Kubernetes clusters inside i d x _ d 8 c c 7 3 e 7 Docker containers.
It was originally designed for testing Kubernetes itself, but has become a popular choice for developers who need
fast, reproducible environments for CI or local i d x _ 1 b 6 c 4 5 7 5 development.
kind requires only i d x _ 6 0 e e a 9 a 6 Docker to be installed. You can install kind with the following:
$ brew install kind # macOS
$ choco install kind # Windows
Then, create a new cluster:
$ kind create cluster --name demo
You should see something like this:
Figure 15.6 – Creating a Kubernetes cluster with kind
485 Introducing Kubernetes
kind will i d x _ 3 5 4 b 1 8 b 8 create multiple Docker containers to simulate the control plane and i d x _ b c 5 7 0 7 c 9 worker nodes of a Kubernetes cluster.
After a minute or two, you can check the status. First, set the correct context for kubectl with this, as indicated in
the preceding output:
$ kubectl cluster-info --context kind-demo
Finally, list your cluster nodes with the following:
$ kubectl get nodes
You should see output similar to this:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION
chunks.content:
NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION
demo-control-plane Ready control-plane 2m v1.32.2
To delete the cluster later, simply run the following:
$ kind delete cluster --name demo
Because i d x _ 6 b d f 4 8 1 8 kind runs entirely in Docker, it is extremely lightweight and i d x _ 8 2 c 2 f 5 0 c portable. It is widely used in automated test
pipelines, GitOps workflows, and scenarios where you need to spin up and tear down clusters quickly.
Choosing the right local environment
All three i d x _ e 1 2 b 5 9 a c options (Docker Desktop, minikube, and kind) are excellent choices for i d x _ 6 1 f 6 2 b 0 b learning Kubernetes. Which one
you use depends on your goals:
Tool Best for Characteristics
Docker Desktop Everyday development
Easiest setup, single node, fully integrated
with Docker
minikube Learning and experimentation Flexible, supports add-ons, VM-based
Understanding kubectl contexts
The kubectl tool can manage multiple Kubernetes clusters. To know which cluster a command should
target, kubectl uses a configuration file called kubeconfig. This file contains one or more contexts, where
each context defines a specific combination of a cluster, a user, and optionally a namespace. Only one
context is active at a time. You can list all available contexts with kubectl config get-contexts and
switch between them using kubectl config use-context <context-name>. This mechanism allows
you to work with several clusters—such as a local development cluster and a production cluster—without
changing your commands.
Note

Regardless of which tool you choose, all examples in this book will work in exactly the same way. Each of these
environments provides a real Kubernetes API and supports all standard resources such as Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services.
With your local cluster now ready, let's start exploring Kubernetes' most fundamental building block: the Pod.
Introduction to Pods
Contrary to what is possible with Docker Compose and Docker Swarm, you cannot run containers directly in a
Kubernetes cluster. In a Kubernetes cluster, you can only run Pods. Pods are i d x _ c 5 0 e b 7 b a the atomic units of Deployment in
Kubernetes. A Pod is an abstraction of one or many co-located containers that share the same Kernel namespaces,
such as the network namespace. No equivalent exists in Docker Swarm. The fact that more than one container can
be collocated and shared with the same network namespace is a very powerful concept. The following diagram
illustrates two Pods:
Figure 15.7 – Kubernetes Pods
In the preceding diagram, we have two Pods, Pod 1 and Pod 2. The first Pod contains two containers, while the
second one only contains a single container. Each Pod gets an IP address assigned by Kubernetes that is unique in
the whole Kubernetes cluster. In our case, these are the following IP addresses: 10.0.12.3 and 10.0.12.5. Both are
part of a private subnet managed by the Kubernetes network driver.
A Pod can contain one or many containers. All those containers share the same Linux kernel namespaces, and in
particular, they share the network namespace. This is indicated by the dashed rectangle surrounding the
containers. Since all containers running in the same Pod share the network namespace, each container needs to
487 Introducing Kubernetes
make sure to use its own port since duplicate ports are not allowed in a single network namespace. In this case, in
Pod 1, the main container is using port 80 while the supporting container is using port 3000.
Requests from other Pods i d x _ 2 d c 3 6 9 8 a or nodes can use the Pod's IP address combined with the corresponding port number to
access the individual containers. For example, you could access the application running in the main container of
Pod 1 through 10.0.12.3:80.
Comparing Docker container networking and Kubernetes Pod
networking
Now, let's compare Docker's i d x _ 1 d c 8 5 2 d f container networking and Kubernetes Pod networking. In the following diagram, we
have Docker i d x _ c 8 3 1 9 5 5 1 on the left-hand side and Kubernetes on the right-hand side:
Figure 15.8 – Containers in a Pod sharing the same network namespace

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 486
chunks.content:
When a Docker container is created, and no specific network is specified, then the Docker engine i d x _ 5 9 8 b f 2 1 a creates a virtual
Ethernet (veth) endpoint. The first container gets veth0, the next one gets veth1, and so on. These virtual Ethernet
endpoints are connected to the Linux bridge, docker0, which Docker automatically creates upon installation.
Traffic is routed from the docker0 bridge to every connected veth endpoint. Every container has its own network
namespace. No two containers use the same namespace. This is on purpose, to isolate applications running inside
the containers from each other.
For a Kubernetes i d x _ 0 7 f 9 d 9 5 9 Pod, the situation is i d x _ 0 f 1 b 8 c b 9 different. When creating a new Pod, Kubernetes first creates a so-called pause
container, the purpose of which is to create and manage the namespaces that the Pod will share with all containers.
Other than that, it does nothing useful; it is just sleeping. The pause container is connected to the docker0 bridge
through veth0. Any subsequent container that will be part of the Pod uses a special feature of the Docker engine
that allows it to reuse an existing network namespace. The syntax to do so looks like this:
$ docker container create --net container:pause ...

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 488
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 488
The important part is the --net argument, which uses container:<container name> as a value. If we create a new
container this way, then Docker does not create a new veth endpoint; the container uses the same one as the pause
container.
Another important consequence of multiple containers sharing the same network namespace is the way they
communicate with each other. Let's consider the following situation—a Pod containing two containers, one
listening at port 80 and the other at port 3000:
Figure 15.9 – Containers in Pods communicating via localhost
When two containers i d x _ 7 9 3 4 1 a a a use the same Linux kernel network namespace, they can communicate with each other
through localhost, similarly to how, when two processes are running on the same host, they can communicate
with i d x _ c b 5 d 1 d 7 6 each other through localhost too.
This is illustrated in the preceding diagram. From the main container, the containerized application inside it can
reach out to the service running inside the supporting container through http://localhost:3000.
Sharing the network namespace
After all this theory, you might be i d x _ 0 f e a 3 0 9 8 wondering how a Pod is actually created by Kubernetes.
Kubernetes only uses what Docker provides. So, how does this network namespace share work? First, Kubernetes
creates the so-called pause container, as mentioned previously.
This container has no other function than to reserve the kernel namespaces for that Pod and keep them alive, even
if no other container inside the Pod is running. Let's simulate the creation of a Pod, then. We start by creating the
pause container, using NGINX for this purpose:
$ docker container run --detach \
--name pause nginx:alpine
Now, we add a second container called main and attach it to the same network namespace as the pause container:
$ docker container run --name main \
-d -it \
489 Introducing Kubernetes
--net container:pause \
alpine:latest ash
Since pause and the sample container are both parts of the same network namespace, they can reach each other
through localhost. To show this, we have to exec into the main container:
$ docker exec -it main /bin/sh
Now, we can test the i d x _ 4 3 6 4 7 c 3 a connection to NGINX running in the pause container and listening on port 80. The following
is what we get if we use the wget utility to do so:
/ # wget -qO – localhost
Doing so gives us this output:
Figure 15.10 – Two containers sharing the same network namespace
The output shows i d x _ 4 0 4 2 e d 9 3 that we can indeed access NGINX on localhost. This is proof that the two containers share the
same namespace. If that is not enough, we can use the ip tool to show eth0 inside both containers, and we will get
the exact same result, specifically, the same IP address, which is one of the characteristics of a Pod where all its

containers share the same IP address:
/ # ip a show eth0
This will show the following output:

The main container didn't get an entry in the Containers list since it is reusing the pause container's endpoint.
Before you continue, please remove the two pause and main containers:
$ docker container rm -f pause main
Next, we will be looking at the Pod life cycle.
491 Introducing Kubernetes
Pod life cycle
Earlier in this book, we learned i d x _ 7 e 8 f 5 a f 3 that containers have a life cycle. A container is initialized, run, and ultimately
exited. When a container exits, it can do this gracefully with an exit code zero, or it can terminate with an error,
which is equivalent to a non-zero exit code.
Similarly, a Pod has a life cycle. Because a Pod can contain more than one container, this life cycle is slightly more
complicated than that of a single container. The life cycle of a Pod can be seen in the following diagram:
Figure 15.12 – The life cycle of Kubernetes Pods
When a Pod is i d x _ e f 2 e 3 5 5 5 created on a cluster node, it first enters the pending status. Once all the containers of the Pod are up
and running, the Pod enters the running status. The pod only enters this state if all its containers run successfully. If
the Pod is asked to terminate, it will request all its containers to terminate. If all containers terminate with exit code
zero, then the Pod enters the succeeded status. This is the happy path.
Now, let's look at some scenarios that lead to the Pod being in a failed state. There are three possible scenarios:
If, during the startup of the Pod, at least one container is not able to run and fails (that is, it exits with a
non-zero exit code), the Pod goes from the pending state into the failed state
If the Pod is in the running state and one of the containers suddenly crashes or exits with a non-zero exit
code, then the Pod transitions from the running state into the failed state
If the Pod is i d x _ 6 7 5 7 8 6 8 4 asked to terminate and, during the shutdown, at least one of the containers exits with a non-
zero exit code, then the Pod also enters the failed state
Now, let's look at the specifications for a Pod.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 490
chunks.content:
Pod specifications
When creating a Pod in a i d x _ d c 5 a a 8 e c Kubernetes cluster, we can use either an imperative or a declarative approach. We
discussed the difference between the two approaches earlier in this book. To rephrase the most important aspect,
using a declarative approach signifies that we write a manifest that describes the end state we want to achieve.
We'll leave out the details of the orchestrator. The end state that we want to achieve is also called the desired state.
•
•
•

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 492
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 492
In general, the declarative approach is strongly preferred in all established orchestrators, and Kubernetes is no
exception.
Thus, in this chapter, we will exclusively concentrate on the declarative approach. Manifests or specifications for a
Pod can be written using either the YAML or JSON formats. In this chapter, we will concentrate on YAML since it is
easier to read for us humans. Let's look at a sample specification. Here is the content of the pod.yaml file, which can
be found in the ch15 subfolder of our labs folder:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: web-pod
spec:
containers:
- name: web
image: nginx:alpine
ports:
- containerPort: 80
Each specification in Kubernetes starts with the version information. Pods have been around for quite some time,
and thus, the API version is v1. The second line specifies the type of Kubernetes object or resource we want to
define. Obviously, in this case, we want to specify a Pod. Next follows a block containing metadata. At a bare
minimum, we need to give the Pod a name. Here, we call it web-pod. The next block that follows is the spec block,
which contains the specification of the pod. The most important part (and the only one in this simple sample) is a
list of all containers that are part of this Pod. We only have one container here, but multiple containers are possible.
The name we chose for our container is web, and the container image is nginx:alpine. Finally, we define a list of
ports the container is exposing.
Once we have authored i d x _ e d 0 e 9 c 5 6 such a specification, we can apply it to the cluster using the Kubernetes CLI, kubectl:
Open a new terminal window and navigate to the ch15 subfolder:
$ cd ~/The-Ultimate-Docker-Contianer-Book-Fourth-Edition
$ cd chapter-15
In this example, we're going to use Docker Desktop's Kubernetes cluster. Thus, make sure that you are
using the right context for the kubectl CLI:
$ kubectl config use-context docker-desktop

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: 1.2 493 Introducing Kubernetes
chunks.content:
1.2 493 Introducing Kubernetes
This will switch the context to our Kubernetes cluster provided by Docker Desktop. Verify with the
following command. If you have more than one context, the one named docker-desktop should be
marked as current:
$ kubectl config get-contexts
In this folder, create a new file called pod.yml and add the Pod specification mentioned earlier in this
section to it. Save the file.
Execute the following command:
$ kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
This will respond with pod "web-pod" created.
We can then list all the Pods in the cluster:
$ kubectl get pods
Doing so will provide us with this output:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE
chunks.content:
NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE
web-pod 1/1 Running 0 9s
As expected, we have one Pod in the Running state. The pod is called web-pod, as defined.
We can get i d x _ a 8 f a 8 5 6 3 more detailed information about the running Pod by using the describe command:
$ kubectl describe pod/web-pod
This gives us something similar to this:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 494
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 494
Figure 15.13 – Describing a Pod running in the cluster
The information i d x _ b 0 a 7 8 8 8 b in the Containers section is very similar to what we find in a docker container inspect output.
Note the pod/web-pod notation in the previous section describe command. Other variants are
possible. For example, pods/web-pod, po/web-pod, pod, and po are aliases of pods.
The kubectl tool defines many aliases to make our lives a bit easier.
The describe command gives us a plethora of valuable information about the Pod, not the least
of which is a list of events that happened and affected this Pod. The list is shown at the end of the
output.
Note
495 Introducing Kubernetes
We can also see a Volumes section with a Projected entry type. It contains the root certificate of the cluster as a
secret. We will discuss Kubernetes secrets in the next chapter. Volumes, on the other hand, will be discussed next.
Pods and volumes
In Chapter 5, Data Volumes and Configuration, i d x _ 8 3 0 0 6 e 5 c we learned about volumes and their purpose: accessing and storing
persistent data. Since containers can mount volumes, Pods can do so as well. In reality, it is really the containers
inside the Pod that mount the volumes, but that is just a semantic detail. First, let's see how we can define a
volume in Kubernetes. Kubernetes supports a plethora of volume types, so we won't delve into too much detail
about this.
Let's just create a local volume implicitly by defining a PersistentVolumeClaim claim called my-data-claim:
Create a file called volume-claim.yaml and add the following specification to it:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
name: my-data-claim
spec:
accessModes:
- ReadWriteOnce
resources:
requests:
storage: 2Gi
We have defined a claim that requests 2 GB of data.
Let's create this claim:
$ kubectl apply -f volume-claim.yaml
This will result in the following output:
persistentvolumeclaim/my-data-claim created
We can list the claim using kubectl (pvc is a shortcut for PersistentVolumeClaim) with the following:
$ kubectl get pvc
This gives us this output:
Figure 15.14 – List of PersistentStorageClaim objects in the cluster
In the output, we can i d x _ b c c 7 1 3 9 b see that the claim has implicitly created a volume called pvc-<ID>.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 496
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 496
Remove the Pod before you continue:
$ kubectl delete pod/web-pod
Alternatively, use the original file defining the Pod with the following command:
$ kubectl delete -f pod.yaml
We are now ready to use the volume created by the claim in a Pod. Let's use a modified version of the Pod
specification that we used previously.
Create a file called pod-with-vol.yaml and add the following specification to it:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: web-pod
spec:
containers:
- name: web
image: nginx:alpine
ports:
- containerPort: 80
volumeMounts:
- name: my-data
mountPath: /data
volumes:
- name: my-data
persistentVolumeClaim:
claimName: my-data-claim
In the last four i d x _ 3 a 1 e 2 f 8 2 lines, in the volumes block, we define a list of volumes we want to use for this Pod. The
volumes that we list here can be used by any of the containers of the Pod. In our particular case, we only
have one volume. We specify that we have a volume called my-data, which is a persistent volume claim
whose claim name is the one we just created.
Then, in the container specification, we have the volumeMounts block, which is where we define the
volume we want to use and the (absolute) path inside the container where the volume will be mounted. In
our case, we mount the volume to the /data folder of the container filesystem.
Let's create this Pod:
$ kubectl apply -f pod-with-vol.yaml

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.content:
4.5 6.
497 Introducing Kubernetes
We can also use the imperative way (not recommended):
$ kubectl create -f pod-with-vol.yaml
Then, we can exec into the container to double-check that the volume has mounted by navigating to
the /data folder, creating a file there, and exiting the container using the following:
$ kubectl exec -it web-pod -- /bin/sh
/ # cd /data
/data # echo "Hello world!" > sample.txt
/data # exit
If we are right, then i d x _ 9 6 9 2 d 0 9 e the data in this container must persist beyond the life cycle of the Pod.
Thus, let's delete the Pod:
$ kubectl delete pod/web-pod
Then, we'll recreate it:
$ kubectl apply -f pod-with-vol.yaml
We'll then exec into the container of the Pod:
$ kubectl exec -it web-pod -- ash
Finally, we output the data:
/ # cat /data/sample.txt
This is the output produced by the preceding command:
Hello world!
It is what we expected.
Exit the container by pressing Ctrl + D.
Delete the Pod before you continue. By now, you should know the command to do so. Otherwise, have a
look back at Step 4.
Also, delete the i d x _ 0 4 8 b f 2 a d persistent volume claim with the following:
$ kubectl delete pvc/my-data-claim

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 498
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 498
Now that we have a good understanding of Pods, let's investigate how those Pods are managed with the help of
ReplicaSets.
Kubernetes ReplicaSet
A single Pod in an environment with high availability requirements is insufficient. What if the Pod crashes? What if
we need to update the application running inside the Pod, but cannot afford any service interruption? These
i d x _ 8 a 5 6 2 0 a e questions and more indicate that Pods alone are not enough, and we need a higher-level concept that can manage
multiple instances of the same Pod. In Kubernetes, the ReplicaSet is used to define and manage such a collection of
identical Pods that are running on different cluster nodes. Among other things, a ReplicaSet defines which
container images are used by the containers running inside a Pod and how many instances of the Pod will run in
the cluster. These properties and many others are called i d x _ 9 9 2 d c 9 9 2 the desired state.
The ReplicaSet is i d x _ 8 3 c c 7 8 5 9 responsible for reconciling the desired state at all times if the actual state ever deviates from it.
Here is a Kubernetes ReplicaSet:
Figure 15.15 – Kubernetes ReplicaSet
In the preceding diagram, we can see a ReplicaSet that governs a number of Pods. The Pods are called pod-api. The
ReplicaSet is responsible for making sure that, at any given time, there is always the desired number of Pods
running. If one of the Pods crashes for whatever reason, the ReplicaSet schedules a new Pod on a node with free
resources instead. If there are more Pods than the desired number, then the ReplicaSet kills superfluous Pods. With
this, we can say that the ReplicaSet guarantees a self-healing and scalable set of Pods. There is no limit to how
many Pods a ReplicaSet can hold.
ReplicaSet specification
Similar to what we i d x _ 8 e 2 a f 5 5 3 have learned about Pods, Kubernetes also allows us to either imperatively or declaratively
define and create a ReplicaSet. Since the declarative approach is by far the most recommended one in most cases,
we're going to concentrate on this approach. Let's work with a sample specification for a Kubernetes ReplicaSet:
Create a new file called replicaset.yaml and add the following content to it:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
name: rs-web
spec:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: 1.499 Introducing Kubernetes
chunks.content:
1.499 Introducing Kubernetes
selector:
matchLabels:
app: web
replicas: 3
template:
metadata:
labels:
app: web
spec:
containers:
- name: nginx
image: nginx:alpine
ports:
- containerPort: 80
This looks an awful lot like the Pod specification we introduced earlier. Let's concentrate on the
differences, then. First, on line 2, we have the kind, which was a Pod, and is now ReplicaSet. Then, on
lines 6–8, we have a selector, which determines the Pods that will be part of the ReplicaSet. In this case, it
is all the Pods that have app as a label with the web value. Then, on line 9, we define how many replicas of
the Pod we want to run—three, in this case. Finally, we have the template section, which i d x _ 6 7 b 5 f e a 4 first defines the
metadata, and then the spec, which defines the containers that run inside the Pod. In our case, we have a
single container using the nginx:alpine image and exporting port 80.
The really important elements are the number of replicas and the selector, which specifies the set of Pods
governed by the ReplicaSet.
Let's use this file to create the ReplicaSet:
$ kubectl apply -f replicaset.yaml
This results in the following:
replicaset "rs-web" created
Now, we list all the ReplicaSets in the cluster (rs is a shortcut for ReplicaSet):
$ kubectl get rs
We get the following:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY AGE
chunks.content:
NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY AGE
rs-web 3 3 3 11s
2.
3.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 500
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 500
In the preceding output, we can see that we have a single ReplicaSet called rs-web, the desired state of
which is 3 (Pods). The current state also shows three Pods and tells us that all three Pods are ready.
We can also list all i d x _ c 8 d 4 0 d 2 8 the Pods in the system:

Kubernetes Deployments
Kubernetes takes the single-responsibility i d x _ 4 6 2 2 6 5 d 0 principle very seriously. All Kubernetes objects are designed to do one
thing and one thing only, and they are designed to do this one thing very well. In this regard, we must understand
Kubernetes ReplicaSets and Deployments. A ReplicaSet, as we have learned, is responsible for achieving and
reconciling the desired state of an application service. This means that the ReplicaSet manages a set of Pods.
A Deployment augments i d x _ e 3 1 e c e e 5 a ReplicaSet by providing rolling updates and rollback i d x _ d c 7 d 6 2 5 2 functionality on top of it. In
Docker Swarm, the Swarm service incorporates the functionality of both ReplicaSet and Deployment. In this
regard, SwarmKit is much more monolithic than Kubernetes. The following diagram shows the relationship of a
Deployment to a ReplicaSet:

Figure 15.17 – Kubernetes Deployment
In the preceding diagram, the ReplicaSet defines and governs a set of identical Pods. The main characteristics of the
ReplicaSet are that it is self-healing, scalable, and always does its best to reconcile the desired state. A Kubernetes
Deployment, in turn, adds rolling updates and rollback functionality to this. In this regard, a Deployment is a
wrapper object for a ReplicaSet.
We will learn more about rolling updates and rollbacks in Chapter 16, Deploying, Updating, and Securing an
Application with Kubernetes.
In the next section, we will learn more about Kubernetes services and how they enable service discovery and
routing.
Kubernetes Services
The moment i d x _ d 5 d 2 2 c a d we start to work with applications consisting of more than one application service, we need service
discovery. The following diagram illustrates this problem:
Figure 15.18 – Service discovery
In the preceding diagram, we have a Web API service that needs access to three other services: payments, shipping,
and ordering. The Web API service should never have to care about how and where to find those three services. In
503 Introducing Kubernetes
the API code, we just want to use the name of the service we want to reach and its port number. A sample would be
http://payments:3000, which is used to access an instance of the payments service.
In Kubernetes, the payments application service is represented by a ReplicaSet of Pods. Due to the nature of highly
distributed systems, we cannot assume that Pods have stable endpoints. A Pod can come and go on a whim. But
that's a problem if we need to access the corresponding application service from an internal or external client. If we
cannot rely on Pod endpoints being stable, what else can we do?
This is i d x _ b c 0 5 1 8 3 5 where Kubernetes Services come into play. They are meant to provide stable endpoints to ReplicaSets or
Deployments, as follows:
Figure 15.19 – Kubernetes service providing stable endpoints to clients
In the preceding diagram, in the center, we can see such a Kubernetes Service. It provides a reliable cluster-wide IP
address, also called i d x _ 2 8 0 5 0 d 7 9 a virtual IP (VIP), as well as a reliable port that's unique in the whole cluster. The Pods that the
Kubernetes Service is proxying are determined by the selector defined in the service specification. Selectors are
always based on labels. Every Kubernetes object can have zero or many labels assigned to it. In our case, the
selector is app=web; that is, all Pods that have a label called app with a value of web are proxied.

Context-based routing
Often, we want to configure i d x _ e 0 8 4 c 2 0 2 context-based routing for our Kubernetes cluster. Kubernetes offers us various ways to
do this. The preferred and most scalable way currently is to use IngressController. The following diagram tries to
illustrate how this ingress controller works:

Chapter 15 510
Figure 15.25 – Context-based routing using a Kubernetes ingress controller
In the preceding diagram, we i d x _ 5 6 7 5 a 4 5 6 can see how context-based (or layer 7) routing works when using an ingress
controller, such as NGINX. Here, we have the Deployment of an application service called web. All the Pods of this
application service have the following label: app=web. Then, we have a Kubernetes Service called web that provides a
stable endpoint to those Pods. The Service has a (virtual) IP of 52.14.0.13 and exposes port 30044. That is, if a
request comes to any node of the Kubernetes cluster for the name web and port 30044, then it is forwarded to this
Service. The Service then load balances the request to one of the Pods.
So far, so good, but how is an ingress request from a client to the http[s]://example.com/web URL routed to our
web service? First, we must define routing from a context-based request to a corresponding <service name>/
<port> request. This is done through an Ingress object:
In the Ingress object, we define the host and path as the source and the (service) name, and the port as
the target. When this Ingress object is created by the Kubernetes API server, then a process that runs as a
sidecar in IngressController picks up this change.
Modifies the i d x _ f e 9 9 2 0 7 2 configuration file of the NGINX reverse proxy.
By adding the new route, NGINX is then asked to reload its configuration, and thus, will be able to
correctly route any incoming requests to http[s]://example.com/web.

With routing and exposure now fully under our control, we've reached a point where managing Kubernetes objects
manually with raw YAML files becomes increasingly cumbersome. In the next section, we'll look at how modern
tools such as GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize simplify this process by introducing reusable templates, declarative
delivery, and automated configuration management.
Popular tools: GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize
By now, you should have a good understanding of Kubernetes' core concepts—how it manages Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services to keep applications running in a desired state. In practice, however, managing all those
YAML manifests manually can quickly become tedious. As your application grows, you might end up maintaining
dozens or even hundreds of configuration files across multiple environments such as development, staging, and
production.
To handle this complexity, the Kubernetes ecosystem has produced a rich collection of complementary tools and
practices that make configuration management, packaging, and deployment easier, safer, and more reproducible.
Among them, three have become particularly popular: GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize.
Let's take a brief look at each.
GitOps: Declarative delivery through version control
Kubernetes was built around the idea of declarative configuration—you describe the desired end state of your
system, and the platform ensures that this state is achieved and maintained. GitOps takes i d x _ 1 e 2 8 3 a 4 1 this principle one step
further by applying it to the entire operational life cycle of a cluster.
In a GitOps workflow, Git becomes the single source of truth for both your application code and your infrastructure
configuration. Every change to the cluster—whether it's a Deployment, a ConfigMap, or a network policy—is
8.
◦
◦
◦
◦
517 Introducing Kubernetes
represented as a commit in a Git repository. Automated agents running inside the cluster continuously monitor
that repository and reconcile any differences between what's declared in Git and what's actually running.
This approach has i d x _ 0 f f a a b 2 5 several powerful advantages:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 516
chunks.content:
Auditability: Every change to the cluster is recorded in Git history, making it easy to track who changed
what and when
Reproducibility: A new cluster can be bootstrapped directly from the same Git repository, guaranteeing
that environments stay consistent
Safety: Changes are applied only after being merged and reviewed, reducing human error and
configuration drift
Automation: Tools such as Argo CD and Flux automatically synchronize cluster state with Git, removing
the need for manual kubectl apply commands
GitOps represents a cultural as well as a technical shift: it merges development and operations practices by making
infrastructure management fully version-controlled, reviewable, and automated. It is now widely considered a
best practice for running production Kubernetes clusters.
Helm 3: The package manager for Kubernetes
If GitOps defines how we manage and deliver i d x _ 8 6 2 3 7 2 1 4 configuration, Helm helps us manage what we deliver. Helm is often
described as the package manager for Kubernetes—similar to apt on Ubuntu or brew on macOS—but instead of
system packages, Helm installs and manages Kubernetes resources.
A Helm package is called a chart. Each chart i d x _ 1 b 1 9 2 3 f 5 bundles together a set of Kubernetes manifests and associated
templates for deploying a specific application or component. Charts can define default values, environment-
specific overrides, dependencies, and life cycle hooks. Using Helm, complex applications can be installed with a
single command:
$ helm install my-app bitnami/nginx
Helm then renders the templates with the provided values, creates the necessary manifests, and applies them to
your cluster.
With Helm 3, the i d x _ f c e 2 7 f c f tool matured significantly. It removed the server-side component (Tiller) introduced in earlier
versions, simplifying security and operations. Helm 3 communicates directly with the Kubernetes API using your
local credentials, integrates seamlessly with RBAC, and supports signed charts for verifying authenticity.
The key benefits i d x _ 3 7 0 0 d b 0 8 of Helm include the following:
Simplicity: Install or upgrade entire applications with a single command
Reusability: Share charts across projects or teams and version them in repositories
Parameterization: Customize deployments easily through values files instead of editing raw YAML
Rollback: Revert to a previous release quickly if an update fails
Helm has become an integral part of modern Kubernetes operations, and most open source applications today
provide official Helm charts for instant deployment.

chunks.heading: Chapter 15 518
chunks.content:
Chapter 15 518
Kustomize: Native configuration customization
While Helm focuses on packaging and reusing application templates, Kustomize addresses i d x _ a 6 1 f 0 9 0 e a different challenge:
how to manage environment-specific differences without duplicating manifests. It allows you to customize
existing YAML files declaratively using overlays, patches, and variable substitutions, all without introducing a
separate templating language.
Kustomize works directly with plain Kubernetes YAML. You start with a base configuration (for example, your
application's Deployment and Service) and then define overlays for specific environments, such as staging or
production. Each overlay can modify only what differs—for instance, image tags, replica counts, or environment
variables—while the rest of the configuration is inherited from the base.
A simple example layout might look like this:
my-app/
├── base/
│ ├── deployment.yaml
│ ├── service.yaml
│ └── kustomization.yaml
└── overlays/
├── staging/
│ └── kustomization.yaml
└── production/
└── kustomization.yaml
To apply a particular overlay, you simply run the following:
$ kubectl apply -k overlays/staging/
Kustomize is i d x _ 8 6 5 a 8 9 f 5 now built directly into kubectl, which means you can use it without installing anything extra. This
makes it a lightweight yet powerful tool for managing variations across multiple environments while keeping your
i d x _ 7 1 a 5 5 b 2 e configuration DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).
Bringing it all together
In practice, these tools are often used together. Helm or Kustomize handle the packaging and customization of
Kubernetes resources, while GitOps provides the automation layer that keeps clusters continuously aligned with
what's defined in Git. Together, they transform Kubernetes from a manual deployment engine into a fully
automated, declarative delivery platform.
As you continue your journey with Kubernetes, you will see these tools and practices appear repeatedly—not just
in small projects, but also in large-scale enterprise environments. They represent the next evolutionary step in
managing infrastructure as code: repeatable, auditable, and fully automated.
519 Introducing Kubernetes
Popular tools summary
In this section, we introduced three of the most widely adopted tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem. GitOps i d x _ 4 0 7 a 4 0 c e extends
declarative management into a fully automated workflow driven by version control. Helm 3 i d x _ e 8 b 2 e 2 8 1 simplifies packaging
and deploying applications through reusable charts. Kustomize i d x _ d 6 3 3 b 9 b f enables clean, environment-specific configuration
without duplicating manifests.
Together, they embody the modern Kubernetes philosophy: automate everything, declare everything, and keep
everything under version control.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 518
chunks.content:
Summary
In this chapter, we took our first deep dive into Kubernetes—the orchestration platform that has become the
foundation of modern cloud-native computing. We began by exploring its architecture, learning how control-
plane and worker nodes collaborate to maintain the cluster's desired state. You discovered how Kubernetes
continuously reconciles what should be running with what is actually running, ensuring resilience and consistency
even in the face of failure.
We then looked at the fundamental building blocks that form the heart of Kubernetes—Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services—and learned how they work together to run, scale, and expose containerized
applications. You also saw how easy it is to get started locally by running Kubernetes on your own machine using
Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind, all of which provide a realistic and fully functional cluster for experimentation.
Finally, we explored the tools and practices that have grown around Kubernetes—GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize
—and saw how they simplify deployment automation and configuration management in real-world
environments. Together, they elevate Kubernetes from a container orchestrator to a complete, declarative delivery
platform.
By now, you should not only understand what Kubernetes is and how it works, but also feel comfortable
experimenting with it locally—deploying simple applications, exploring the API, and observing how the system
keeps everything in harmony.
In the next chapter, we will build upon this foundation and move from theory to practice. You will learn how to
deploy, update, and secure an application on Kubernetes, exploring concepts such as rolling updates, scaling
strategies, and secret management within a running cluster. This is where Kubernetes truly comes to life—as a
living, self-healing platform that empowers you to deliver applications reliably at any scale.

chunks.content:
10.521 Introducing Kubernetes
Answers
Here are some exemplary answers to the preceding questions:
Kubernetes solves the challenge of running containerized applications reliably and at scale. It
automatically schedules workloads, manages resources, and ensures that the desired number of
containers are always running. Unlike traditional manual deployments, Kubernetes uses a declarative
model and a control loop to reconcile desired and actual state continuously.
The main components of Kubernetes are the control plane (which includes the API server, controller
manager, scheduler, and etcd) and the worker nodes (which run Pods through the kubelet and container
runtime). The control plane makes global decisions about the cluster, while worker nodes execute those
decisions by running the workloads.
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It can contain one or more tightly coupled containers
that share networking and storage. While Docker focuses on individual containers, Kubernetes Pods
group containers that need to communicate and operate together as a single unit.
Docker Desktop, minikube, and kind all run local Kubernetes clusters but differ in setup and purpose.
Docker Desktop provides the easiest integrated option for developers. minikube uses a lightweight VM or
container backend and supports add-ons for experimentation. kind runs entirely inside Docker
containers and is ideal for testing and CI/CD pipelines.
Declarative configuration means defining the desired end state of your application or infrastructure—for
example, how many replicas should exist or which image should be used—instead of giving step-by-step
commands. Kubernetes continuously ensures that the actual state matches this desired state, which
makes systems more predictable and self-healing.
GitOps applies declarative management to the entire delivery process. Configuration and deployments
are stored in Git, which becomes the single source of truth. Tools such as Argo CD or Flux continuously
reconcile the running cluster state with what's stored in Git, ensuring reproducibility, auditability, and
automation.
A Helm chart is a reusable package that bundles all Kubernetes manifests required to deploy an
application. Helm allows you to parameterize configurations, manage dependencies, and perform
upgrades or rollbacks with a single command, greatly simplifying application life cycle management.
Kustomize lets you modify existing YAML manifests declaratively using overlays and patches, without
introducing a separate templating language. This makes it ideal for maintaining multiple environments
(for example, development, staging, and production) while keeping configurations consistent and DRY.
Helm, Kustomize, and GitOps complement each other. Helm provides reusable packaging, Kustomize

chunks.content:
enables clean customization, and GitOps automates synchronization and delivery. Together, they form a
powerful ecosystem for managing applications at scale with minimal manual intervention.
To set up your own local cluster, choose one of the supported environments (for example, Docker
Desktop or minikube). Install kubectl, verify the cluster with kubectl get nodes, create a simple YAML
manifest for an NGINX Pod, and apply it using kubectl apply -f. Observe how Kubernetes schedules
and manages your Pod automatically.

523 Introducing Kubernetes
16
Deploying, Updating, and Securing
an Application with Kubernetes
In the previous chapter, we explored the fundamental building blocks of Kubernetes and learned how they work
together to define, run, and scale containerized workloads. We looked at the control plane and worker nodes,
studied Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, and Services, and gained a solid understanding of how Kubernetes
maintains the desired state of workloads.
Now, it's time to put all that knowledge into practice. In this chapter, we will deploy a complete, multi-service
application to a Kubernetes cluster, update it without interruption, and secure it using built-in Kubernetes
mechanisms. You will learn how Kubernetes enables continuous delivery through rolling updates, how it checks
and maintains the health of your workloads through liveness, readiness, and startup probes, and how to protect
sensitive information using Kubernetes Secrets.
Beyond functionality, we will also look at security best practices that every Kubernetes operator and developer
should follow—covering topics such as Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), network isolation, workload identity,
and secret management. Security is now an integral part of the deployment process rather than an afterthought,
and Kubernetes provides several mechanisms to help enforce it consistently.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to do the following:
Deploy a multi-service application into a Kubernetes cluster
Define and use liveness, readiness, and startup probes to ensure high availability (HA)
Perform rolling and blue-green updates with zero downtime
Apply essential Kubernetes security best practices for production readiness
In short, you will learn how to deliver reliable, resilient, and secure applications on Kubernetes—skills that form
the foundation for running containerized workloads in the cloud, which we will explore in the next chapter.

Technical requirements
In this chapter, we will deploy and update a small multi-service application named TaskBoard on a local
Kubernetes cluster. To follow along, you need a working Docker environment and at least one local Kubernetes
option installed. The examples in this chapter have been tested on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
You can use any of the following local setups introduced in the previous chapter:
minikube: Recommended for this chapter. Provides a fully featured single-node cluster ideal for
experimentation.
Docker Desktop with Kubernetes: Convenient option if you already use Docker Desktop.

kind (Kubernetes in Docker): Lightweight and popular for CI environments.
Make sure that you have the following software installed and available on your system:
Docker Engine (24.x or newer): Required for building and pushing container images.
kubectl: The official Kubernetes command-line interface. Verify the installation with the following
command:
$ kubectl version --client
minikube v1.33 or newer (if you are using minikube). You can verify this with the following command:
$ minikube version
Git: To clone the book's sample repository.
A code editor such as Visual Studio Code for editing YAML manifests.
To prepare your working environment, navigate to your local clone of the book's GitHub repository and create a
new subfolder for this chapter:
$ cd ~/The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition
$ mkdir chapter-16 && cd chapter-16
The sample files for this chapter are located in the chapter-16/solutions folder of the repository. You will find all
Kubernetes manifests for the TaskBoard application there, including definitions for the frontend, backend, and
database components.
With your environment ready, let's put Kubernetes to work. In the next section, we will deploy the TaskBoard
application step by step, starting with its backend API service and database, followed by the web frontend. Along
the way, we'll see how each component is defined declaratively, how Kubernetes maintains its desired state
automatically, and how simple commands let us observe what's happening inside the cluster.

Deploying our first application
In this walk-through, you'll deploy TaskBoard, a small three-component application:
frontend: A static web UI served by NGINX
api: A REST backend (containerized service)
db: PostgreSQL with persistent storage
We'll proceed i d x _ 3 9 e 1 d 1 4 0 incrementally so that you can validate each step before moving on:
Start your local cluster: If you're using minikube (recommended), do this using the following
commands:
$ minikube start
$ kubectl cluster-info
$ kubectl get nodes
Using Docker Desktop or kind is fine as well. Where commands differ (e.g., exposing Services), notes are
included.
Build the Docker images: In the solutions folder under task-board, you'll find the sample code for the
TaskBoard application. Please analyze the code—we are not going to discuss it in detail in this chapter as
it is outside of scope. Let's use this code to build the Docker images for api and frontend that we will
need later in this hands-on example:
$ minikube image build -t taskboard-api:1.0.0 \
./solutions/task-board/api
$ minikube image build -t taskboard-frontend:1.0.0 \
./solutions/task-board/frontend
This build will take a moment, so please be patient.
Create a dedicated namespace: Keep chapter resources isolated and easy to clean up later:
$ kubectl create namespace taskboard
$ kubectl config set-context \
--current --namespace=taskboard
$ kubectl get ns

by default. Therefore, we do not always have to specify it in our subsequent kubectl commands.
